title: The seven books (the deuterocanon)
hook: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1–2 Maccabees are in Catholic Bibles; many Protestants call them the Apocrypha

segments.voice: Yesterday, the furnace song, every creature called to praise. Your line was all ye works, bless the lord. That song is part of today's story.

Put a Catholic Bible and a Protestant Bible side by side and count the books. The Catholic one has seventy-three: forty-six in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New, as the Catechism counts them. The Protestant one will usually have sixty-six; the Westminster Confession, a Protestant statement of faith, lists them by name. The New Testaments match exactly. The difference is all in the Old Testament: seven books, plus extra passages in Esther and Daniel, like yesterday's song from the furnace. Same faith in Christ, same Gospels, and a different-sized shelf. So how did that happen?
screen: `SEVENTY-THREE OR SIXTY-SIX.` → `THE NEW TESTAMENTS MATCH.` → `SEVEN BOOKS, AND SOME PASSAGES.`

segments.voice: The seven are Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and First and Second Maccabees. Catholics call them deuterocanonical. Canon comes from the Greek kanon, a straight rod for measuring, and so a rule, and so the list of books measured as scripture. Deutero means second. Not second-rate: their place in the list was settled later, after some discussion. Catholics hold them to be inspired scripture, fully. The history, as plainly as possible. Before Jesus, Jews in the Greek-speaking world used a Greek translation of their scriptures, the Septuagint, and its collections included these books. The early Church, mostly Greek-speaking, read that Bible. North African councils around the year 400 list them as scripture. Saint Jerome, translating from the Hebrew, had doubts and set them in a separate category, though he translated some anyway. In his German Bible, Martin Luther gathered them into a section between the Testaments, calling them Apocrypha: not held equal to scripture, but useful and good to read. The Council of Trent in 1546 answered by defining the Catholic canon with all seven included. The first King James Bible printed them too, between the Testaments; later printings could leave them out. Today the Jewish Bible doesn't include them. The Orthodox churches include them and a few more. Protestant confessions like Westminster don't count them as scripture; the Church of England's Articles say they are read for example of life, but not to establish doctrine. In a Catholic Bible they sit right in among the others. Over the next week, this path opens four of them.
screen: `KANON: A MEASURING ROD.` · `SECOND, NOT SECOND-RATE.` · `SEPTUAGINT, JEROME, LUTHER, TRENT.` · `WHO READS THEM, AND HOW.` · then, large: `THE BOOKS BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: If you have a Catholic Bible nearby, open the contents: Tobit comes after Nehemiah, which the Douay calls Second Esdras, with Judith next; read just its first verse. If not, picture the shelf, forty-six books, seven you may never have opened. If you pray, ask for a little curiosity about the pages you've never read.
Deuterocanonical. The seven Old Testament books, and parts of Esther and Daniel, whose place in the canon was settled later; Catholics receive them as scripture. Today's word.
Your line: the books between. Seven books, and a longer shelf than you thought. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear readings from the deuterocanonical books at Mass, at weddings (Tobit), funerals (Wisdom) and in the prayers for the dead (2 Maccabees), the same as any other book of scripture.

chat.says: Why does your Catholic Bible have more books than mine?
options: It keeps seven books from the early Church's Greek Bible as scripture.
The Council of Trent wrote seven new books in 1546 to add to it.
Catholic Bibles add extra Gospels that other churches never accepted.
chat.meaning: The seven deuterocanonical books came from the Septuagint the early Church read. Trent defined them as canon; Protestant Bibles usually leave them out.

kanon.meaning: Greek: a measuring rod, a rule

Septuagint.meaning: the Greek translation of the Jewish scriptures

Apocrypha.meaning: Luther's name: books good to read, not equal to scripture

Council of Trent.meaning: the council that defined the Catholic canon in 1546

Westminster Confession.meaning: a Protestant statement of faith that lists the books

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): book counts now tied to sources (CCC 120 for 46 + 27; the Westminster Confession's list for 66) instead of 'most Protestant Bibles'; cut the uncited 'sixteenth-century term' date; Lutherans no longer credited with the Anglican Article VI wording ('example of life'); added sources for Luther's Bible, the 1611 KJV and the Articles; 'most Catholic Bibles' placement softened and the Douay's 'Second Esdras' named; flippant fork option 'burn them' replaced.
Book counts: Catholic 73 (46 OT + 27 NT), most Protestant 66 (39 + 27). Confirm.
'Deuterocanonical' is usually credited to Sixtus of Siena (Bibliotheca Sancta, 1566); the script says only 'the sixteenth century'. Confirm.
Luther's 1534 complete Bible placed these books between the Testaments with the heading describing them as not held equal to scripture, but useful and good to read; paraphrased. Confirm.
Anglican Article VI: the Church reads them 'for example of life and instruction of manners'; paraphrased as 'for example of life'. Confirm wording is fair for Lutherans too, or limit to Anglicans.
Orthodox canons include additional books (e.g. 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, Psalm 151, Prayer of Manasseh); 'a few more' used. Confirm.
Jerome's view: he distinguished these books in his prefaces but translated Tobit and Judith; confirm the summary.
Placement of Tobit after Nehemiah holds for most modern Catholic Bibles (NAB, RSV-CE, Jerusalem); in the Douay it follows 2 Esdras (Nehemias). Confirm.
